q: A biology tutor writes four statements on the board comparing prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. Which of the statements is accurate?
o: Prokaryotes divide by mitosis and eukaryotes by binary fission.
Prokaryotic DNA is linear and eukaryotic DNA is one circular loop.
Bacteria have peptidoglycan walls and plants have cellulose walls.
Prokaryotic ribosomes are 80S and eukaryotic ribosomes are 70S.
w: Bacteria (prokaryotes) build their cell walls from peptidoglycan, and plants (eukaryotes) build theirs from cellulose. Each of the other statements reverses a real difference: ribosome size (prokaryotes 70S, eukaryotes 80S), method of division and form of the DNA.

n.0: This reverses the methods: prokaryotes divide by binary fission and eukaryotes use mitosis or meiosis.
n.1: This reverses the DNA forms: prokaryotes usually have one circular chromosome and eukaryotes have several linear chromosomes.
n.3: This reverses the sizes: prokaryotes have smaller 70S ribosomes and eukaryotes have 80S ribosomes.

q: A lab manual describes cell walls built from cellulose, chitin and peptidoglycan. Which pairing of wall material and cell is correct?
o: Cellulose in the wall of a bacterial cell
Cellulose in the wall of a yeast cell
Peptidoglycan in the wall of a plant cell
Chitin in the wall of a mold cell
w: Molds and yeasts are fungi, and fungal cell walls are made of chitin. Plant walls are cellulose and bacterial walls are peptidoglycan.

n.0: Bacterial walls are made of peptidoglycan, not cellulose.
n.1: Yeast is a fungus, so its wall contains chitin rather than the cellulose found in plants.
n.2: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose. Peptidoglycan is the bacterial wall material.

q: A cell has a membrane-bound nucleus, mitochondria and a cell wall, but no chloroplasts. Of the following, which is the most likely source of this cell?
o: A yeast cell
A Staphylococcus bacterium
A moss leaf cell
A human liver cell
w: Step 1: a nucleus and mitochondria mean the cell is eukaryotic, which rules out bacteria. Step 2: a cell wall without chloroplasts fits a fungus such as yeast, which has a chitin wall and cannot photosynthesize.

n.1: Bacteria have cell walls but are prokaryotes, so they have no nucleus or mitochondria.
n.2: A moss leaf cell has a wall and nucleus, but as a photosynthetic leaf cell it contains chloroplasts.
n.3: Human cells are eukaryotic with mitochondria, but animal cells have no cell wall.

q: A student is comparing a typical plant cell with a typical animal cell. Which structures are found in the plant cell but not in the animal cell? Select all that apply.
o: Mitochondria for respiration
Ribosomes that make proteins
Large central vacuole
Chloroplasts
Centrioles near the nucleus
Cell wall made of cellulose
w: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole that animal cells lack. Both cell types have mitochondria and ribosomes.

n.0: Plant cells have mitochondria too; they respire as well as photosynthesize.
n.1: Ribosomes are found in every cell, plant, animal and prokaryotic.
n.4: Centrioles are usually found in animal cells, not plant cells, so they are the reverse of what is asked.

q: A microbe from a hot spring lacks a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, yet genetic testing shows it is not a bacterium. How should it be classified?
o: As a virus, since it lacks organelles
As a eukaryote in the protist group
As a fungus, since it has a cell wall
As a prokaryote in domain Archaea
w: Prokaryotes include two groups, Bacteria and Archaea. A cell with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles that is not a bacterium is an archaeon.

n.0: Viruses are not cells at all. This microbe is a cell with ribosomes and a membrane, so it is not a virus.
n.1: Protists are eukaryotes, so they have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
n.2: Fungi are eukaryotes with a nucleus, so a cell without a nucleus cannot be a fungus.

q: A researcher compares the DNA of a bacterium with the DNA of a human white blood cell. Which description fits the bacterial DNA?
o: A single circular chromosome, often with plasmids
Several linear chromosomes inside a nuclear envelope
Linear chromosomes coiled around histone proteins
RNA in place of DNA, packed inside a protein capsid
w: Bacteria usually carry one circular chromosome in the nucleoid region, often with small extra circles of DNA called plasmids.

n.1: Multiple linear chromosomes in a nucleus describe the human (eukaryotic) cell, not the bacterium.
n.2: Histone packaging into chromatin is a eukaryotic feature.
n.3: Some viruses carry RNA inside a capsid. Bacteria are cells and store their genes in DNA.

q: A study guide sorts organisms into prokaryotes and eukaryotes by their cell structure. Which statement from the guide is accurate?
o: Bacteria and fungi are both prokaryotic organisms.
Plants are eukaryotes, but fungi are prokaryotic cells.
Protists are prokaryotes since most are single-celled.
Plants, animals, fungi and protists are all eukaryotes.
w: Eukaryotes include animals, plants, fungi and protists. Prokaryotes are the bacteria and archaea.

n.0: Fungi are eukaryotes with a nucleus. Only the bacteria in this pair are prokaryotes.
n.1: Fungi are eukaryotic, with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
n.2: Being single-celled does not make an organism prokaryotic. Protists such as amoebas have a nucleus.

q: A student argues that bacteria cannot make ATP because they have no mitochondria. Which response best corrects the student?
o: Bacteria make ATP on ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
Bacteria make ATP by glycolysis in the cytoplasm.
Bacteria make ATP inside their chloroplasts.
Bacteria make ATP inside the nuclear envelope.
w: Step 1: glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and needs no organelle. Step 2: every cell, including a bacterium, has cytoplasm, so a prokaryote can make ATP without mitochondria.

n.0: Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis. They use energy to build proteins rather than produce ATP.
n.2: Chloroplasts are membrane-bound organelles, which prokaryotes lack.
n.3: Prokaryotes have no nucleus, so they have no nuclear envelope.

q: Cells of the pancreas secrete large amounts of protein-based digestive enzymes into the small intestine. Which organelle would be especially extensive in these cells?
o: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Peroxisomes
Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Lysosomes
w: Rough ER is studded with ribosomes and makes and folds proteins destined for secretion, so cells that export a lot of protein have extensive rough ER.

n.0: Smooth ER has no ribosomes. It makes lipids and steroids and detoxifies drugs, so it suits steroid-secreting or liver cells.
n.1: Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and toxins and convert hydrogen peroxide; they do not produce secreted proteins.
n.3: Lysosomes digest worn-out organelles and engulfed material inside the cell; they do not make secreted proteins.

q: Liver cells of a patient who takes a daily anticonvulsant drug show a marked increase in an organelle that detoxifies drugs and makes lipids. Which organelle is it?
o: Golgi apparatus
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Nucleolus
w: Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and carries out lipid and steroid synthesis and detoxification, which is why it is prominent in liver cells exposed to drugs.

n.0: The Golgi modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids; it does not detoxify drugs.
n.2: Rough ER makes proteins on its ribosomes; detoxification and lipid synthesis are smooth ER jobs.
n.3: The nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosome subunits inside the nucleus.

q: A researcher damages a dense region inside the nucleus of a cultured cell, and the cell soon stops assembling new ribosomes. Which structure was most likely damaged?
o: The centrosome
The nucleolus
The nuclear envelope
The Golgi apparatus
w: The nucleolus is the dense region inside the nucleus that makes ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosome subunits.

n.0: The centrosome sits in the cytoplasm and organizes microtubules and the spindle.
n.2: The nuclear envelope is the double membrane around the nucleus, not a dense region inside it, and it does not build ribosomes.
n.3: The Golgi is in the cytoplasm and packages proteins; it does not make ribosomal RNA.

q: On a quiz, a student writes that the Golgi apparatus makes proteins. Which correction describes the role of the Golgi accurately?
o: It breaks down proteins with hydrolytic enzymes.
It synthesizes lipids and steroid hormones.
It modifies and packages proteins made elsewhere.
It copies DNA into messenger RNA for export.
w: Proteins are made by ribosomes (many on rough ER). The Golgi then modifies, sorts and packages them into vesicles, like a post office.

n.0: Breaking down material with hydrolytic enzymes is the job of lysosomes.
n.1: Lipid and steroid synthesis happens in the smooth ER.
n.3: Copying DNA into mRNA is transcription, which takes place in the nucleus.

q: Heart muscle cells contract continuously throughout life and need a steady supply of ATP. Compared with less active cells, which organelle would these cells contain in especially large numbers?
o: Mitochondria
Lysosomes
Peroxisomes
Ribosomes
w: Mitochondria carry out aerobic cellular respiration and make most of a cell's ATP, so highly active cells such as cardiac and skeletal muscle cells contain many of them.

n.1: Lysosomes digest worn-out parts and engulfed particles; they do not supply ATP.
n.2: Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and hydrogen peroxide but are not the main ATP producers.
n.3: Ribosomes make proteins. ATP production is the job of mitochondria.

q: A neutrophil engulfs a bacterium, enclosing it in a vesicle. Which organelle then fuses with the vesicle and digests the bacterium using hydrolytic enzymes in an acidic interior?
o: Golgi apparatus
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Peroxisome
Lysosome
w: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes in an acidic interior and digest engulfed bacteria, food particles and worn-out organelles.

n.0: The Golgi packages proteins and makes lysosomes, but it does not itself digest engulfed bacteria.
n.1: Smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies drugs; it does not digest engulfed microbes.
n.2: Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and toxins and convert hydrogen peroxide with catalase; they are not the acidic digestive sacs.

q: Cells lining the trachea move a layer of mucus and trapped particles up toward the throat. Which structures on the surface of these cells produce this movement?
o: A single long flagellum on each cell
Many short cilia on each cell
Centrioles anchored at the cell surface
Microfilaments in the cell wall
w: Cilia are many short, hairlike projections that beat together, as in the airway. Flagella are one or a few long whips, as on sperm.

n.0: Flagella are long and usually single, and they propel a cell such as a sperm rather than sweeping material across a surface.
n.2: Centrioles organize microtubules and the spindle; they do not themselves beat to move mucus.
n.3: Human cells have no cell wall, and microfilaments are not the beating surface structures in the airway.

q: A cancer drug blocks the assembly of microtubules from tubulin. Which cell process would this drug most directly interfere with?
o: Synthesis of steroids in the smooth ER
Formation of the mitotic spindle
Production of ATP on the cristae
Synthesis of ribosomal RNA
w: Microtubules form the spindle fibers that move chromosomes during cell division, so blocking them stops dividing cells, which is why such drugs are used against cancer.

n.0: Steroid synthesis is carried out by smooth ER enzymes, not by the cytoskeleton.
n.2: ATP is made by the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane, not by microtubules.
n.3: Ribosomal RNA is made in the nucleolus and does not depend on microtubule assembly.

q: Which observation provides the strongest support for the hypothesis that mitochondria descended from prokaryotes engulfed by an ancestral cell?
o: They have their own circular DNA and a double membrane.
They produce most of the ATP made by the cell.
They are found in plant cells as well as animal cells.
They are more numerous in muscle cells than in skin cells.
w: Endosymbiotic theory is supported by features mitochondria share with bacteria: their own circular DNA and ribosomes, a double membrane, and division by binary fission.

n.1: Producing most of the ATP is the function of mitochondria, not evidence of where they came from.
n.2: Being present in plants and animals is true, but it says nothing about a prokaryotic origin.
n.3: Higher numbers in active cells reflect energy demand, not ancestry.

q: The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is folded into many cristae. What is the main advantage of this folding for the cell?
o: It anchors ribosomes that make secreted proteins.
It gives the electron transport chain more area.
It holds chlorophyll for capturing light energy.
It stores calcium ions for muscle contraction.
w: The electron transport chain sits in the inner membrane (cristae) and makes most of the cell's ATP, so more folds mean more membrane for ATP production.

n.0: Ribosomes making secreted proteins are attached to the rough ER.
n.2: Chlorophyll is held in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts, not mitochondria.
n.3: Calcium storage for contraction is the job of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, a smooth ER in muscle.

q: A student is listing the structures in a plant leaf cell that contain their own DNA. Which structures should be on the list? Select all that apply.
o: Golgi apparatus
Ribosome
Nucleus
Chloroplast
Mitochondrion
Lysosome
w: The nucleus holds the cell's chromosomes, and mitochondria and chloroplasts each carry their own small circular DNA (evidence for endosymbiotic origin).

n.0: The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages proteins and has no genome of its own.
n.1: Ribosomes are made of ribosomal RNA and protein. They read mRNA but contain no DNA.
n.5: Lysosomes are enzyme-filled sacs made by the Golgi and have no DNA.

q: A pancreatic cell makes a digestive enzyme and releases it into a duct. Place the structures in the order the enzyme passes through them, starting with where it is made.
o: Golgi apparatus
Secretory vesicle
Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Transport vesicle
Plasma membrane (exocytosis)
Ribosome on the rough ER
w: A secreted protein is made by a ribosome on the rough ER, enters the rough ER to be folded, travels in a transport vesicle to the Golgi for modification and packaging, leaves in a secretory vesicle, and is released when that vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane by exocytosis.

q: Oxygen moves from the alveoli, where its concentration is high, into lung capillary cells by passing directly through the phospholipid bilayer. Which transport process does this describe?
o: Facilitated diffusion through channels
Active transport by membrane pumps
Simple diffusion
Osmosis through aquaporins
w: Small nonpolar molecules such as O₂ and CO₂ cross the bilayer directly, from high to low concentration, with no protein and no ATP: simple diffusion.

n.0: Facilitated diffusion needs a channel or carrier protein. Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it passes through the lipid bilayer itself.
n.1: Active transport uses ATP to move substances against a gradient. Oxygen is moving down its gradient.
n.3: Osmosis is the movement of water, not of a dissolved gas such as oxygen.

q: Glucose enters a muscle cell through GLUT carrier proteins, moving from a higher concentration in the blood to a lower concentration in the cell. No ATP is used. Which process is this?
o: Pinocytosis by vesicles
Active transport by a pump
Facilitated diffusion
Simple diffusion across the bilayer
w: Movement down a concentration gradient through a carrier or channel protein, without ATP, is facilitated diffusion.

n.0: Pinocytosis takes in droplets of fluid by vesicle and uses ATP; it is not carrier-mediated transport of single molecules.
n.1: Active transport uses ATP and moves substances from low to high concentration. A carrier protein alone does not make transport active.
n.3: Simple diffusion passes straight through the bilayer with no protein. Glucose is too large and polar to do that.

q: In a lab, red blood cells are placed in a 5% sodium chloride solution, which is hypertonic to the cells. What will most likely happen to the cells?
o: There is no net water movement, so the cells keep their shape.
Water enters the cells, which swell and undergo hemolysis.
Sodium enters the cells, which swell as solute builds up.
Water leaves the cells, which shrink and undergo crenation.
w: A hypertonic solution has more solute outside the cell, so water leaves by osmosis and the red blood cells shrink (crenation).

n.0: No net water movement describes an isotonic solution such as 0.9% NaCl, not a 5% solution.
n.1: Swelling and hemolysis happen in a hypotonic solution, where water moves into the cell.
n.2: Osmosis is the movement of water, not solute. The cells lose water and shrink.

q: A selectively permeable membrane separates a 2% sucrose solution on side A from a 10% sucrose solution on side B. Sucrose cannot cross the membrane. What net movement will occur?
o: Sucrose moves from side B to side A.
Neither water nor sucrose will move.
Water moves from side A to side B.
Water moves from side B to side A.
w: Step 1: side B has the higher solute concentration, so it has the lower water concentration. Step 2: in osmosis water moves toward the higher solute concentration, so the net flow is from A to B.

n.0: The stem states sucrose cannot cross, and osmosis moves water rather than solute.
n.1: Water can still cross the membrane. The sucrose difference drives osmosis even though sucrose itself cannot move.
n.3: Water moves toward the side with more solute (B), not away from it.

q: A nursing student is reviewing the sodium-potassium pump in the plasma membrane of a resting neuron. Which statement about the pump is accurate?
o: It uses ATP to move both ions against their gradients.
It moves 2 Na⁺ out and 3 K⁺ in during each cycle.
It is facilitated diffusion, since it uses a carrier protein.
It moves both ions down their concentration gradients.
w: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump is active transport: it spends ATP to push Na⁺ out and K⁺ in, each from low to high concentration.

n.1: The numbers are reversed: the pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in.
n.2: Using a carrier protein does not make transport passive. The pump uses ATP, which facilitated diffusion does not.
n.3: Movement down a gradient needs no ATP. The pump works against both gradients.

q: A wilted lettuce leaf is soaked in pure tap water and becomes crisp again within an hour. Which explanation best accounts for this change?
o: Water enters the cells, which then swell until they lyse and collapse.
Solutes enter the cells by active transport, so the cells shrink.
Water leaves the cells, and plasmolysis pulls the membranes inward.
Water enters the cells, and the walls let them become turgid.
w: Pure water is hypotonic to the leaf cells, so water enters by osmosis. The cellulose wall resists the swelling, and the cells become turgid (firm) instead of bursting.

n.0: Animal cells such as red blood cells lyse in hypotonic solutions. Plant cells are protected by the cell wall.
n.1: Solute gain would draw water in, not make the cells shrink, and pure water has almost no solute to take up.
n.2: Plasmolysis happens in a hypertonic solution, when water leaves the cell. That would make the leaf wilt more.

q: A patient receives intravenous fluid of 0.9% sodium chloride rather than sterile pure water. Which statement best explains this choice at the level of the red blood cells?
o: It is hypotonic, so water moves into dehydrated red cells.
It is isotonic, so red cells neither gain nor lose water overall.
It supplies the sodium that red cells absorb by active transport.
It is hypertonic, so excess water is drawn out of the red cells.
w: Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) is isotonic to human cells, so there is no net water movement and the red cells keep their shape. Pure water is hypotonic and would cause hemolysis.

n.0: 0.9% NaCl is isotonic, not hypotonic. Pure water is the hypotonic fluid that would make red cells swell and burst.
n.2: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves sodium out of cells, not in, and the choice of saline is about tonicity.
n.3: 0.9% NaCl is not hypertonic. A hypertonic fluid would make red cells shrink (crenation).

q: LDL particles carrying cholesterol bind to specific proteins on the surface of a liver cell, and the membrane then folds inward to bring them in. Which process is this?
o: Phagocytosis of a large particle
Exocytosis by a secretory vesicle
Receptor-mediated endocytosis
Facilitated diffusion via a carrier
w: Binding of a specific substance to surface receptors followed by inward folding of the membrane into a vesicle is receptor-mediated endocytosis, the route for cholesterol (LDL).

n.0: Phagocytosis is endocytosis of large particles such as bacteria by cells such as neutrophils, not receptor-specific uptake of LDL.
n.1: Exocytosis releases material from the cell; this material is entering.
n.3: Facilitated diffusion moves single molecules through channels or carriers, without forming vesicles.

q: A nursing student is matching membrane processes to examples for a study sheet. Which pairing is correct?
o: Facilitated diffusion: the pump that moves Na⁺ and K⁺ ions
Active transport: oxygen moving into a red blood cell
Exocytosis: a neuron releasing neurotransmitter from vesicles
Phagocytosis: a cell taking in droplets of extracellular fluid
w: Exocytosis releases material from the cell when a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, as in neurotransmitter, hormone and enzyme secretion.

n.0: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to move ions against their gradients, which is active transport.
n.1: Oxygen enters red blood cells by simple diffusion down its gradient, with no ATP.
n.3: Taking in fluid droplets is pinocytosis (cell drinking). Phagocytosis engulfs solid particles such as bacteria.

q: A student sets up a model in which a dye diffuses across a membrane from a concentrated solution into a dilute one. Which change would increase the rate of diffusion?
o: Using a dye that has much larger molecules
Making the membrane twice as thick as before
Diluting the more concentrated solution
Raising the temperature of the solutions
w: Diffusion is faster at higher temperature, with a steeper concentration gradient, smaller molecules, greater surface area and a shorter distance.

n.0: Larger molecules diffuse more slowly than smaller ones.
n.1: A thicker membrane increases the distance, which slows diffusion.
n.2: Diluting the concentrated side makes the gradient less steep, which slows diffusion.

q: A textbook diagram labels the plasma membrane of an animal cell as a fluid mosaic. Which description of the membrane is consistent with this model?
o: A rigid layer of cellulose that small solutes pass through
A phospholipid bilayer that ions cross with no protein help
A double layer of proteins coated with phospholipid heads
A phospholipid bilayer with proteins that drift within it
w: The fluid mosaic model describes a phospholipid bilayer in which proteins, cholesterol (in animal cells) and glycoproteins are embedded and can move laterally, forming a selectively permeable barrier.

n.0: A cellulose layer describes a plant cell wall, which lies outside the plasma membrane.
n.1: Ions are charged and cannot easily cross the hydrophobic interior; they need channel or carrier proteins.
n.2: The membrane's framework is a phospholipid bilayer, with proteins embedded in it, not a protein double layer.

q: A physiology handout lists several ways substances cross cell membranes. Which of these processes require the cell to spend ATP? Select all that apply.
o: Neutrophil engulfing a bacterium
Glucose entering by GLUT carriers
Carbon dioxide leaving a cell
Sodium-potassium pump moving ions
Pancreatic cell secreting an enzyme
Water crossing through aquaporins
w: Active transport (the Na⁺/K⁺ pump), endocytosis (phagocytosis by a neutrophil) and exocytosis (enzyme secretion) all use ATP. Diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis are passive.

n.1: Glucose moving down its gradient through GLUT carriers is facilitated diffusion, which needs no ATP.
n.2: CO₂ leaves by simple diffusion down its concentration gradient, with no ATP.
n.5: Water crossing through aquaporins is osmosis, a passive process.

q: A researcher tracks the DNA content of a dividing skin cell and finds that it doubles before any chromosomes become visible under the microscope. During which phase did this doubling occur?
o: The G1 phase of interphase
The S phase of interphase
Prophase of mitosis
The G2 phase of interphase
w: DNA is replicated during the S (synthesis) phase of interphase, turning each chromosome into two sister chromatids before mitosis begins.

n.0: G1 is a growth phase before DNA synthesis begins.
n.2: In prophase the already-replicated chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes; replication happened earlier, in S phase.
n.3: G2 follows S phase. The DNA is already doubled, and the cell is preparing to divide.

q: A slide of an onion root tip shows a cell in which identical sets of condensed chromosomes are being pulled toward opposite ends of the cell. Which phase of mitosis is shown?
o: Anaphase
Telophase
Prophase
Metaphase
w: In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles, so two identical sets of chromosomes are seen moving apart.

n.1: In telophase the chromosomes have reached the poles, nuclear envelopes re-form and chromosomes decondense.
n.2: In prophase chromosomes condense and the spindle forms; chromatids have not yet separated.
n.3: In metaphase the chromosomes are lined up at the cell's equator, not moving toward the poles.

q: A human skin cell with 46 chromosomes completes mitosis and cytokinesis. Which result is expected?
o: Two identical cells, each with 46 chromosomes
Four haploid cells, each with 23 chromosomes
Four diploid cells, each genetically different
Two haploid cells, each with 23 chromosomes
w: Mitosis produces 2 genetically identical diploid daughter cells: 46 chromosomes in, 46 in each daughter cell.

n.1: Four haploid cells is the result of meiosis, which makes gametes, not of mitosis in a skin cell.
n.2: Mitosis makes two cells, not four, and they are genetically identical to the parent.
n.3: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same; it does not halve it.

q: During anaphase I of meiosis in a human testis, which structures separate and move to opposite poles of the cell?
o: Single chromatids drawn from all four strands of each tetrad
Haploid daughter cells pinched apart at a cleavage furrow
Homologous chromosomes, each still made of two chromatids
Sister chromatids, each becoming its own chromosome
w: Anaphase I separates homologous chromosomes; each still consists of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. Sister chromatids separate later, in anaphase II.

n.0: The four chromatids of a tetrad do not split up individually in anaphase I; whole homologs, each with two chromatids, move apart.
n.1: Pinching apart the cytoplasm is cytokinesis, which follows telophase; it is not what moves to the poles in anaphase I.
n.3: Sister chromatids separate in anaphase II of meiosis and in mitotic anaphase, not in anaphase I.

q: Two sisters with the same parents differ genetically partly because segments were exchanged between homologous chromosomes while their parents' gametes formed. When does this exchange take place?
o: Metaphase of mitosis
Prophase II of meiosis
Anaphase I of meiosis
Prophase I of meiosis
w: Crossing over happens in prophase I, when homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) as tetrads and exchange segments.

n.0: Homologous chromosomes do not pair in mitosis, so there is no crossing over.
n.1: Homologs are no longer paired in prophase II, so crossing over between them does not occur then.
n.2: Anaphase I is when homologs separate; the exchange had already happened in prophase I.

q: During meiosis I in a woman's ovary, the two copies of chromosome 21 fail to separate, and both end up in the egg. A normal sperm fertilizes this egg. What will the zygote most likely have?
o: 47 chromosomes, including three copies of chromosome 21
47 chromosomes, with an XXY set of sex chromosomes
45 chromosomes, with one copy of chromosome 21
45 chromosomes, the pattern seen in Turner syndrome
w: Step 1: nondisjunction gives the egg 24 chromosomes, including two copies of chromosome 21. Step 2: adding a normal sperm's 23 gives 47, with three copies of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21, Down syndrome).

n.1: XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) involves the sex chromosomes, but the nondisjunction here involved chromosome 21.
n.2: A zygote with one chromosome 21 would come from an egg that received no copy. Here the egg received both copies.
n.3: Turner syndrome (45,X) is a missing sex chromosome. This egg has an extra chromosome, so the total rises above 46.

q: A student compares mitosis and meiosis in a table. Which event occurs in meiosis but does not occur in mitosis?
o: Replication of DNA before division
Pairing of homologous chromosomes
Separation of sister chromatids
Formation of a spindle from microtubules
w: Homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) and form tetrads only in prophase I of meiosis. The other events happen in both processes.

n.0: DNA is replicated once, during S phase, before both mitosis and meiosis.
n.2: Sister chromatids separate in mitotic anaphase and in anaphase II of meiosis.
n.3: A microtubule spindle moves chromosomes in both mitosis and meiosis.

q: A karyotype is prepared from a body cell of a healthy human female. Which description of her chromosomes is accurate?
o: 22 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of X chromosomes
23 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of X chromosomes
22 pairs of autosomes plus one X and one Y chromosome
46 pairs of chromosomes, including two X chromosomes
w: Human body cells have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes, XX in a female.

n.1: This adds up to 24 pairs (48 chromosomes). There are 22 pairs of autosomes, not 23.
n.2: An X and a Y is the male sex chromosome pair.
n.3: Humans have 46 chromosomes, which is 23 pairs, not 46 pairs.

q: At the end of mitosis, a plant root cell divides its cytoplasm differently from an animal cell. Which structure forms between the two new plant cells?
o: A nuclear envelope that splits the cell
A centriole pair that pulls the cell apart
A cleavage furrow that pinches inward
A cell plate that becomes a new wall
w: In plant cells, cytokinesis builds a cell plate across the middle that develops into a new cell wall. Animal cells pinch in with a cleavage furrow.

n.0: Nuclear envelopes re-form around each set of chromosomes in telophase; they do not divide the cytoplasm.
n.1: Most plant cells lack centrioles, and centrioles organize the spindle rather than splitting the cytoplasm.
n.2: A cleavage furrow is how animal cells divide their cytoplasm; the rigid plant wall prevents pinching.

q: Two children of the same parents are not genetically identical. Which processes contribute to this genetic variation? Select all that apply.
o: Identical copying of chromosomes in mitosis
Formation of the mitotic spindle
Crossing over during prophase I
Independent assortment of homologous pairs
Division of the cytoplasm in cytokinesis
Random fertilization of an egg by one sperm
w: Crossing over (prophase I), independent assortment of homologous pairs (metaphase I) and random fertilization all shuffle alleles, so siblings differ. Mutation adds further variation.

n.0: Mitosis produces genetically identical cells, so it does not create variation among offspring.
n.1: The spindle moves chromosomes in both mitosis and meiosis but does not shuffle alleles.
n.4: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm; it does not change which alleles a cell carries.

q: Place the events of mitosis in the order they occur in a dividing animal cell, starting with the first.
o: A cleavage furrow completes division of the cytoplasm.
Chromosomes line up along the cell's equator.
Nuclear envelopes re-form and chromosomes decondense.
Chromatin condenses into chromosomes and the spindle forms.
Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
w: Prophase (chromosomes condense, spindle forms), metaphase (chromosomes line up at the metaphase plate), anaphase (sister chromatids separate), telophase (nuclear envelopes re-form), and cytokinesis, which overlaps telophase and finishes last.

q: Place these events of meiosis in the order they occur during the formation of sperm cells, starting with the first.
o: Homologous pairs line up at the cell's equator.
Homologous chromosomes separate to opposite poles.
Single chromosomes line up at the equator of each new cell.
Sister chromatids separate to opposite poles.
Homologous chromosomes pair up and cross over.
w: Meiosis I: prophase I (synapsis and crossing over), metaphase I (homologous pairs line up), anaphase I (homologs separate). Meiosis II: metaphase II (chromosomes line up singly), anaphase II (sister chromatids separate), giving four haploid cells.

q: During a sprint, a runner's leg muscle cells run short of oxygen. Which stage of glucose breakdown can continue to supply these cells with ATP?
o: The Krebs cycle in the matrix
Glycolysis in the cytoplasm
The Calvin cycle in the stroma
The electron transport chain
w: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and needs no oxygen, netting 2 ATP per glucose. With lactic acid fermentation regenerating what glycolysis needs, it keeps running when oxygen is short.

n.0: The Krebs cycle depends on the electron transport chain, which needs oxygen, so it slows when oxygen runs short.
n.2: The Calvin cycle is part of photosynthesis in plant chloroplasts, not a pathway in human muscle.
n.3: The electron transport chain requires oxygen as the final electron acceptor, so it stops without oxygen.

q: A student writes that the Krebs cycle produces most of the ATP in aerobic cellular respiration. Which stage actually produces the most ATP per molecule of glucose?
o: Pyruvate oxidation in the matrix
Lactic acid fermentation
Glycolysis in the cytoplasm
The electron transport chain
w: The electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae) uses NADH and FADH2 from earlier stages to make most of the 30 to 38 ATP per glucose.

n.0: Pyruvate oxidation releases CO₂ and makes NADH but produces little ATP directly.
n.1: Fermentation is anaerobic and yields only the 2 ATP from glycolysis.
n.2: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP per glucose, a small share of the total.

q: A patient breathes in oxygen that eventually reaches the mitochondria of her cells. What is the role of this oxygen in aerobic cellular respiration?
o: It accepts electrons from the chain and forms water.
It is released as a product of the light reactions.
It splits glucose into two molecules of pyruvate.
It combines with carbon to form carbon dioxide.
w: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain; it picks up electrons and hydrogen ions to form water.

n.1: Release of oxygen by the light reactions is part of photosynthesis, not respiration.
n.2: Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate without using any oxygen.
n.3: The CO₂ exhaled comes from carbon in glucose released during pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle, not from the oxygen breathed in.

q: Bread dough rises when yeast cells, deprived of oxygen inside the dough, break down sugar and release a gas. Which process is responsible, and what does it produce?
o: Aerobic respiration, producing water and oxygen gas
Lactic acid fermentation, producing lactic acid and CO₂
Photosynthesis, producing glucose and oxygen gas
Alcoholic fermentation, producing ethanol and CO₂
w: Without oxygen, yeast carry out alcoholic fermentation: glycolysis followed by conversion of pyruvate to ethanol and carbon dioxide. The CO₂ bubbles make the dough rise.

n.0: The yeast lack oxygen, and aerobic respiration consumes oxygen rather than producing it.
n.1: Lactic acid fermentation occurs in human muscle and releases no CO₂, so it would not raise dough.
n.2: Yeast are fungi and cannot photosynthesize; photosynthesis also uses CO₂ rather than releasing it.

q: In a leaf cell, water molecules are split and oxygen gas is released during photosynthesis. Where in the chloroplast does this happen?
o: In the inner membrane, during electron transport
In the thylakoids, during the light reactions
In the cytoplasm, during glycolysis
In the stroma, during the Calvin cycle
w: The light-dependent reactions take place in the thylakoid membranes. There water is split, O₂ is released, and ATP and NADPH are made for the Calvin cycle.

n.0: Electron transport on an inner membrane that ends with O₂ forming water describes mitochondria, the reverse of releasing O₂.
n.2: Glycolysis in the cytoplasm is part of respiration and neither splits water nor releases oxygen.
n.3: The Calvin cycle in the stroma fixes CO₂ into sugar; it does not split water.

q: A plant biology quiz asks about the light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle) of photosynthesis. Which statement about the Calvin cycle is accurate?
o: It requires darkness and stops once light is present.
It releases CO₂ in the matrix of the mitochondria.
It splits water and releases oxygen in the thylakoids.
It fixes CO₂ into sugar using ATP and NADPH.
w: The Calvin cycle takes place in the stroma and uses the ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to fix carbon dioxide into sugar.

n.0: Light-independent means it does not use light directly. It runs in daylight, powered by ATP and NADPH from the light reactions.
n.1: Releasing CO₂ in the mitochondrial matrix describes the Krebs cycle of respiration.
n.2: Splitting water and releasing O₂ happen in the light-dependent reactions in the thylakoids.

q: A teacher asks the class to compare cellular respiration with photosynthesis in a green plant. Which statement is accurate?
o: Respiration happens in chloroplasts and photosynthesis in mitochondria.
Respiration releases CO₂ and photosynthesis releases O₂.
Respiration releases O₂ and photosynthesis releases CO₂.
Plants carry out photosynthesis instead of cellular respiration.
w: Respiration: glucose + O₂ -> CO₂ + H₂O + ATP. Photosynthesis: CO₂ + H₂O + light -> glucose + O₂. The equations are roughly reversed, and plants do both.

n.0: The organelles are reversed: respiration uses mitochondria and photosynthesis uses chloroplasts.
n.2: The gases are reversed: respiration uses O₂ and releases CO₂, and photosynthesis does the opposite.
n.3: Plants have mitochondria and carry out cellular respiration as well as photosynthesis.

q: Energy for a muscle contraction is released when a cell converts ATP into ADP and an inorganic phosphate. Which bond is broken in this reaction?
o: The peptide bond inside the adenine ring
The bond between ribose and the first phosphate
The bond holding the last phosphate group
The bond between adenine and ribose
w: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) releases usable energy when the bond to its last (third) phosphate is hydrolyzed, giving ADP + Pi.

n.0: Peptide bonds join amino acids in proteins; ATP is a nucleotide and has none.
n.1: Losing the first phosphate would remove all three phosphates at once, not form ADP.
n.3: Breaking the adenine-ribose bond would destroy the nucleoside rather than form ADP.

q: Most leaves look green in sunlight. Which statement best explains this in terms of how chlorophyll interacts with light?
o: It absorbs mostly red and blue light and reflects green.
It absorbs mostly green light and reflects red and blue.
It absorbs mostly green light and turns it into glucose.
It absorbs ultraviolet light and gives it off as green.
w: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue wavelengths for photosynthesis and reflects green, which is the color we see.

n.1: This is reversed. A pigment looks the color it reflects, so green is the color chlorophyll absorbs least.
n.2: Green light is mostly reflected, so it contributes little energy to making glucose.
n.3: Leaves are green because of reflected green light, not because chlorophyll converts ultraviolet light into green.

q: A toxin blocks the electron transport chain in a patient's cells. Which change in those cells would be expected?
o: Glucose is broken down directly into CO₂ in the cytoplasm.
Oxygen use rises, as more is needed to accept electrons.
ATP output rises, as glycolysis no longer competes for glucose.
ATP output drops, and cells shift to lactic acid fermentation.
w: Step 1: the electron transport chain makes most of the cell's ATP, so blocking it causes a sharp fall in ATP. Step 2: cells fall back on glycolysis, which needs no oxygen, regenerating its needs by lactic acid fermentation.

n.0: CO₂ is released in the mitochondria (pyruvate oxidation and Krebs cycle), not from glucose in the cytoplasm.
n.1: Oxygen is used only as the final electron acceptor of the chain, so a blocked chain uses less oxygen, not more.
n.2: Glycolysis makes only 2 ATP per glucose, so losing the chain lowers ATP output; it does not raise it.

q: A muscle cell completely breaks down one molecule of glucose by aerobic cellular respiration. Which of these are products of the process? Select all that apply.
o: Molecular oxygen
Carbon dioxide
ATP
Lactic acid
Glucose
Water
w: Aerobic respiration: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ -> 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + energy (ATP and heat).

n.0: Oxygen is a reactant of aerobic respiration; it is released by photosynthesis.
n.3: Lactic acid is made by fermentation when oxygen is lacking, not by complete aerobic breakdown.
n.4: Glucose is the fuel (reactant) being broken down, not a product.

q: Place the steps of aerobic cellular respiration in the order they occur as one molecule of glucose is broken down, starting with the first.
o: The Krebs cycle releases CO₂ and makes NADH and FADH2.
Oxygen accepts the electrons and water is formed.
Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is oxidized.
Glucose is split into two pyruvate in the cytoplasm.
Electrons pass along the chain on the cristae, making most ATP.
w: Glycolysis (cytoplasm) -> pyruvate oxidation -> Krebs cycle (matrix; CO₂ released, NADH and FADH2 made) -> electron transport chain on the inner membrane (most ATP) -> oxygen as the final electron acceptor forms water.

q: A student builds a model of one DNA nucleotide for a biology display. Which three components should the model include?
o: An amino group, a carboxyl group and an R group
A phosphate group, a ribose sugar and a nitrogenous base
A phosphate group, deoxyribose and a nitrogenous base
Glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate group
w: A nucleotide is a phosphate group + a 5-carbon sugar + a nitrogenous base. In DNA the sugar is deoxyribose.

n.0: An amino group, carboxyl group and R group are the parts of an amino acid, the monomer of proteins.
n.1: Ribose is the sugar in RNA nucleotides; DNA uses deoxyribose.
n.3: Glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate make up a phospholipid, not a nucleotide.

q: A lab analysis of a nucleic acid sample detects the bases adenine, guanine, cytosine and uracil. Which other feature would this molecule be expected to have?
o: Thymine bases paired with adenine
Deoxyribose as the sugar in each nucleotide
A double helix held by A-T base pairs
Ribose as the sugar in each nucleotide
w: Uracil marks the molecule as RNA. RNA nucleotides contain the sugar ribose, and RNA is usually single-stranded.

n.0: RNA has uracil in place of thymine; uracil pairs with adenine.
n.1: Deoxyribose is the sugar of DNA. A molecule containing uracil is RNA.
n.2: A double helix with A-T pairs describes DNA, which contains thymine, not uracil.

q: When a DNA sample is gently heated, its two strands separate, yet each strand's sugar-phosphate backbone stays intact. Which bonds were broken?
o: Glycosidic bonds between the sugars
Peptide bonds between nucleotides
Hydrogen bonds between paired bases
Phosphodiester bonds in the backbone
w: The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases (2 for A-T, 3 for G-C). The backbone is held by strong covalent phosphodiester bonds, which stay intact.

n.0: Glycosidic bonds join sugars in carbohydrates; DNA strands are not held together this way.
n.1: Peptide bonds join amino acids in proteins, not nucleotides.
n.3: Phosphodiester bonds form the backbone, which the stem says stayed intact.

q: One strand of a DNA molecule has the sequence 5'-ATGCCA-3'. Which sequence is the complementary strand, written in the same left-to-right alignment?
o: 3'-ACCGTA-5'
3'-UACGGU-5'
3'-GCATTG-5'
3'-TACGGT-5'
w: In DNA, A pairs with T and G pairs with C, and the strands are antiparallel. So 5'-ATGCCA-3' pairs with 3'-TACGGT-5'.

n.0: This is the original strand written backward, not its complement.
n.1: Uracil is found in RNA, not DNA; this is what an mRNA copy would look like.
n.2: This pairs A with G and T with C, which is not how DNA bases pair.

q: The DNA double helix has the same width along its entire length. Which feature of base pairing explains this uniform width?
o: Each base pair joins a purine with a pyrimidine.
Adenine pairs with guanine, both double-ring bases.
Each base pair joins two single-ring pyrimidines.
Each base pair joins two double-ring purines.
w: Every pair joins a double-ring purine (A or G) with a single-ring pyrimidine (T or C), so each rung of the ladder is the same width.

n.1: Adenine pairs with thymine, not guanine; A-G pairing is a common error.
n.2: Two pyrimidines would make a pair narrower; each pair contains one purine.
n.3: Two purines would make a pair wider than the others; A pairs with T and G pairs with C.

q: A short segment of double-stranded DNA contains 4 guanine-cytosine pairs and 6 adenine-thymine pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold its two strands together?
w: Step 1: G-C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds and A-T pairs have 2. Step 2: (4 x 3) + (6 x 2) = 12 + 12 = 24.

n.0: 30 counts every pair as having 3 hydrogen bonds; A-T pairs have 2.
n.1: 20 counts every pair as having 2 hydrogen bonds; G-C pairs have 3.
n.3: 26 swaps the bond numbers: (4 x 2) + (6 x 3) gives 26.

q: During protein synthesis, one type of RNA carries a specific amino acid and has a three-base anticodon. Which type of RNA is this?
o: Messenger RNA
Transfer RNA
Ribosomal RNA
Primer RNA
w: Transfer RNA (tRNA) carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon that pairs with the matching mRNA codon at the ribosome.

n.0: mRNA carries the codons copied from DNA. It does not carry amino acids, and the anticodon is on tRNA.
n.2: rRNA is the structural and catalytic part of ribosomes; it does not carry amino acids or anticodons.
n.3: Primer RNA is the short strand primase lays down to start DNA replication; it carries no amino acid.

q: A researcher sequences the stretch of chromosome 7 that holds the instructions for making the CFTR protein. Which term best describes this stretch of DNA?
o: A codon
A genome
A chromosome
A gene
w: A gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a protein (or a functional RNA).

n.0: A codon is three bases that code for one amino acid; a whole protein needs many codons.
n.1: A genome is all of an organism's DNA, not one protein-coding segment.
n.2: Chromosome 7 is the whole DNA molecule; the CFTR instructions are one stretch of it.

q: A textbook describes the two strands of a DNA double helix as antiparallel. What does this term mean?
o: The two strands run in opposite directions.
One strand is made of DNA and the other of RNA.
The strands are joined by covalent bonds between bases.
The two strands have exactly the same base sequence.
w: Antiparallel means the two strands run in opposite directions: one runs 5' to 3' and its partner runs 3' to 5'.

n.1: Both strands of the double helix are DNA. DNA-RNA pairing happens only briefly during transcription.
n.2: Bases are joined across the strands by hydrogen bonds; that describes bonding, not direction.
n.3: The strands are complementary (A-T, G-C), not identical in sequence.

q: A student is filling in a chart that compares DNA with RNA. Which features do DNA and RNA have in common? Select all that apply.
o: The sugar deoxyribose in each nucleotide
The base uracil in place of thymine
A double-stranded helical shape
Phosphate groups in the backbone
The bases guanine and cytosine
The base adenine
w: Both nucleic acids have a sugar-phosphate backbone and the bases A, G and C. DNA has deoxyribose and thymine and is double-stranded; RNA has ribose and uracil and is usually single-stranded.

n.0: Deoxyribose is found in DNA only; RNA contains ribose.
n.1: Uracil is found in RNA, where it replaces the thymine of DNA.
n.2: DNA is a double helix, but RNA is usually single-stranded.

q: Analysis of a sample of double-stranded DNA shows that 22% of its bases are thymine. What percentage of its bases are guanine? Enter your answer as a whole-number percent.

tr.22: assumed guanine equals thymine instead of adenine
tr.56: found G + C but did not split it between G and C
tr.78: subtracted thymine once from 100 and stopped

w: Step 1: A = T, so A is also 22%, and A + T = 44%. Step 2: G + C = 100% - 44% = 56%. Step 3: G = C, so G = 56% / 2 = 28%.

q: A double-stranded DNA fragment contains 400 bases in total, and 120 of them are cytosine. How many of the bases are adenine? Enter a whole number.

tr.160: found A + T but did not halve it

w: Step 1: C = G, so there are 120 guanine as well, and G + C = 240. Step 2: A + T = 400 - 240 = 160. Step 3: A = T, so adenine = 160 / 2 = 80.

q: A liver cell begins making albumin by copying the albumin gene into messenger RNA. Where does this step take place, and which enzyme carries it out?
o: In the nucleus, by DNA polymerase
In the cytoplasm, by helicase
At the ribosome, by RNA polymerase
In the nucleus, by RNA polymerase
w: Copying DNA into mRNA is transcription. In eukaryotes it happens in the nucleus, where RNA polymerase reads the DNA template strand and builds complementary mRNA.

n.0: DNA polymerase copies DNA into DNA during replication, not DNA into RNA.
n.1: Helicase unwinds DNA during replication; transcription happens in the nucleus, not the cytoplasm.
n.2: The ribosome is the site of translation, not transcription.

q: A segment of the DNA template strand reads 3'-TAC-5'. Which mRNA codon is transcribed from it, and what is that codon's role?
o: UAC, copied directly from the template
AUG, the start codon for methionine
AUG, a stop codon that ends translation
ATG, a codon read at the ribosome
w: Base pairing gives T->A, A->U, C->G, so 3'-TAC-5' is transcribed into 5'-AUG-3'. AUG is the start codon and codes for methionine.

n.0: Transcription makes a complementary copy, not an identical one; UAC is the matching tRNA anticodon.
n.2: AUG is the start codon. The stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA.
n.3: mRNA contains uracil, not thymine, so the codon cannot be ATG.

q: Before a newly made pre-mRNA leaves the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell, it is processed. Which change occurs during this processing?
o: Introns are removed and exons are joined.
Codons are translated into amino acids.
Thymine bases are replaced by uracil.
Exons are removed and introns are joined.
w: During processing, introns (noncoding regions) are cut out and exons (coding regions) are spliced together; a 5' cap and poly-A tail are also added.

n.1: Translation happens later, at ribosomes in the cytoplasm, after the mRNA leaves the nucleus.
n.2: RNA is built with uracil from the start; no thymine is present in pre-mRNA to replace.
n.3: This is reversed: introns are removed and exons are kept.

q: A cell copies its DNA during S phase. After one round of replication, what does each of the two new DNA double helices contain?
o: Original and new pieces mixed in each strand
Two newly made strands, with no old DNA
Two original strands, rejoined together
One original strand and one new strand
w: DNA replication is semiconservative: each strand serves as a template, so every new double helix keeps one original strand and gains one new strand.

n.0: Mixed pieces within each strand would be dispersive replication, which was ruled out experimentally.
n.1: If both helices were entirely new, the original DNA would be lost; each helix keeps one parent strand.
n.2: Two original strands rejoined would be conservative replication, which is not how DNA copies.

q: In sickle cell anemia, a single base substitution in the beta-globin gene causes valine to replace glutamic acid in the hemoglobin chain. Which type of mutation is this?
o: Nonsense mutation
Frameshift mutation
Missense mutation
Silent mutation
w: A missense mutation is a point substitution that changes one amino acid to a different one, as in sickle cell (glutamic acid to valine).

n.0: A nonsense mutation creates a stop codon and shortens the protein; here the chain is full length with one amino acid changed.
n.1: A frameshift results from inserting or deleting bases, not from substituting one base.
n.3: A silent mutation leaves the amino acid unchanged; here the amino acid changes.

q: Which of the following mutations in the coding region of a gene is most likely to change every amino acid after the mutation site?
o: Deletion of three adjacent bases
Deletion of a single base
A substitution that keeps the same amino acid
A substitution that changes one amino acid
w: Step 1: codons are read in groups of three. Step 2: deleting one base (not a multiple of three) shifts the reading frame, so every downstream codon is misread: a frameshift.

n.0: Deleting three bases removes one codon (one amino acid) and keeps the reading frame intact downstream.
n.2: A silent substitution does not change the amino acid at all.
n.3: A missense substitution changes only one amino acid; the reading frame is unaffected.

q: The mRNA codons GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG all code for the amino acid glycine. Which property of the genetic code does this illustrate?
o: Universality: nearly all organisms share the same code
Redundancy: several codons can specify one amino acid
Punctuation: stop codons mark where a protein ends
Ambiguity: one codon can specify several amino acids
w: The genetic code is redundant (degenerate): 61 codons code for 20 amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one codon.

n.0: The code is nearly universal, but the example is about multiple codons for glycine, not about different organisms.
n.2: Stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) code for no amino acid; the example involves codons for glycine.
n.3: The code is unambiguous: each codon specifies one meaning. The example shows several codons for one amino acid, the reverse.

q: A point mutation changes one amino acid in the sequence of a digestive enzyme, and the enzyme stops working. Which explanation is most likely?
o: The new amino acid removed the gene's stop codon.
The new amino acid blocked transcription of the gene.
The new amino acid kept mRNA from leaving the nucleus.
The new amino acid changed the folding and shape.
w: The amino acid sequence (primary structure) determines how the chain folds into its 3-D shape, and shape determines function. One changed amino acid can alter the active site.

n.0: Stop codons are part of the mRNA, not the protein, so an amino acid cannot remove one.
n.1: A changed amino acid is a feature of the finished protein; it cannot act back on transcription of the gene.
n.2: The protein is made after mRNA leaves the nucleus, so its amino acids cannot affect mRNA export.

q: A student is sorting statements about protein synthesis. Which statements correctly describe translation? Select all that apply.
o: It takes place inside the nucleus of the cell.
RNA polymerase reads the DNA template strand.
Introns are cut out and exons are joined.
The ribosome joins amino acids with peptide bonds.
It takes place at ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
tRNA anticodons pair with mRNA codons.
w: Translation happens at ribosomes in the cytoplasm: mRNA codons are read, tRNA anticodons pair with them to deliver amino acids, and the ribosome joins the amino acids with peptide bonds.

n.0: The nucleus is the site of transcription; translation happens in the cytoplasm.
n.1: RNA polymerase reading DNA is transcription.
n.2: Removing introns is mRNA processing, which happens in the nucleus before translation.

q: Place the steps in the order they occur as a eukaryotic cell makes a protein from one of its genes, starting with the first.
o: The mature mRNA leaves the nucleus and binds a ribosome.
RNA polymerase transcribes the gene into pre-mRNA.
Introns are removed and the exons are spliced together.
The ribosome reads the start codon AUG.
tRNAs deliver amino acids and peptide bonds form.
The ribosome reaches a stop codon and releases the chain.
w: Transcription in the nucleus (RNA polymerase) -> processing (introns out, exons spliced) -> mRNA exits to a ribosome -> translation begins at AUG -> tRNAs bring amino acids and peptide bonds form -> a stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA) ends translation and the polypeptide is released.

q: Place the events of DNA replication in the order they occur at a replication fork, starting with the first.
o: DNA ligase joins the Okazaki fragments together.
Helicase unwinds the helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds.
Primase lays down a short RNA primer.
DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides.
w: Helicase unzips the double helix; primase adds an RNA primer; DNA polymerase extends from the primer, adding complementary nucleotides 5' to 3' and proofreading; on the lagging strand the resulting Okazaki fragments are joined by DNA ligase.

q: The coding region of an mRNA, from the start codon AUG through the stop codon, is 450 nucleotides long. How many amino acids will the resulting polypeptide contain? Enter a whole number.

tr.150: counted the stop codon as an amino acid
tr.450: assumed one nucleotide per amino acid

w: Step 1: each codon is 3 nucleotides, so 450 / 3 = 150 codons. Step 2: the last codon is a stop codon, which codes for no amino acid, so 150 - 1 = 149 amino acids.

q: A pea plant has purple flowers and the genotype Pp, where P (purple) is dominant over p (white). Which statement about this plant is correct?
o: It is heterozygous, and purple is its phenotype.
It is homozygous, and Pp is its phenotype.
It is heterozygous, and purple is its genotype.
It carries two different genes for flower color.
w: Pp has two different alleles, so the plant is heterozygous. Its genotype is Pp; its observable trait (phenotype) is purple flowers.

n.1: Homozygous means two identical alleles (PP or pp), and Pp is a genotype, not a phenotype.
n.2: Genotype and phenotype are swapped: Pp is the genotype and purple is the phenotype.
n.3: Pp is two different alleles of one gene, not two different genes.

q: A breeder owns a black guinea pig, where black (B) is dominant over white (b), and wants to know whether it is BB or Bb. Which cross would best answer this question?
o: Cross it with a heterozygous black (Bb) guinea pig.
Cross it with a white (bb) guinea pig.
Cross it with another black guinea pig of unknown genotype.
Cross it with a homozygous black (BB) guinea pig.
w: A test cross pairs the unknown dominant-phenotype individual with a homozygous recessive (bb). Any white offspring prove the unknown parent carries b, so it is Bb.

n.0: A Bb partner passes on b only half the time, so white pups appear less often (1/4 instead of 1/2 if the unknown is Bb). It is a weaker test than crossing with bb.
n.2: An unknown partner adds a second unknown, so the results cannot be interpreted.
n.3: Every offspring of a BB parent shows black whatever the other parent is, so the cross cannot reveal a hidden b allele.

q: A black guinea pig, where black (B) is dominant over white (b), is crossed with a white guinea pig. The litter has 5 black and 4 white pups. What is the genotype of the black parent?
o: bb, because white pups appeared in the litter
BB, because black is the dominant allele
BB, because most of the pups are black
Bb, because some of the pups are white
w: Step 1: a white pup is bb and must get b from each parent. Step 2: the black parent therefore carries b, so it is Bb. The roughly 1:1 ratio matches the Bb x bb test cross.

n.0: A bb parent would itself be white, but this parent is black.
n.1: Black being dominant tells you the parent has at least one B, not that it has two.
n.2: A BB parent could pass on only B, so every pup would be black; the white pups rule this out.

q: A heterozygous tall pea plant (Tt) forms pollen grains, and each grain carries either T or t but never both. Which principle explains this?
o: The law of independent assortment
The law of dominance
Codominance of the two alleles
The law of segregation
w: The law of segregation: the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation (meiosis), so each gamete carries one allele.

n.0: Independent assortment concerns alleles of different genes sorting independently, not the two alleles of one gene separating.
n.1: The law of dominance explains why a Tt plant looks tall, not how its alleles are split into gametes.
n.2: Codominance is a pattern in which both alleles are expressed in the phenotype; it does not describe gamete formation.

q: A geneticist studies pairs of genes in fruit flies. Which pair of genes would be least likely to follow Mendel's law of independent assortment?
o: Two genes, one on the X chromosome and one on an autosome
Two genes lying next to each other on one chromosome
Two genes at opposite ends of one long chromosome
Two genes on different chromosomes that both affect eye color
w: Independent assortment holds for genes on different chromosomes, and nearly so for genes far apart on one chromosome, because crossing over separates them. Genes right next to each other are linked and are usually inherited together.

n.0: The X chromosome and an autosome are different chromosomes, so these genes assort independently.
n.2: Genes far apart on one chromosome are separated by crossing over so often that they assort almost independently. Adjacent genes rarely are.
n.3: Genes on different chromosomes assort independently even when they influence the same trait.

q: Two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt x Tt) are crossed, where tall is dominant over short. What is the expected phenotype ratio among the offspring?
o: 3 tall : 1 short
1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt
1 tall : 1 short
1 tall : 2 medium : 1 short
w: Tt x Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. TT and Tt both look tall, so the phenotype ratio is 3 tall : 1 short.

n.1: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt is the genotype ratio, not the phenotype ratio.
n.2: 1 : 1 is the result of a test cross (Tt x tt), not of Tt x Tt.
n.3: A 1 : 2 : 1 phenotype ratio with an intermediate form comes from incomplete dominance. Here tall is completely dominant, so Tt plants are tall.

q: Two parents are both carriers (Aa) of an autosomal recessive disorder. Their first three children are unaffected. What is the chance that their fourth child will be affected?
o: Very high, since three children are already unaffected
3 in 4, since that is the share expected to show the trait
1 in 16, using the product rule across two children
1 in 4, the same as for each of the earlier children
w: Each fertilization is independent. For Aa x Aa, every child has a 1/4 chance of being aa, whatever happened with earlier children.

n.0: A 3:1 ratio is a probability for each child, not a quota the family must fill.
n.1: 3/4 is the chance a child is unaffected (AA or Aa), not affected.
n.2: The product rule gives the chance of two specified events together; the question asks about one child.

q: True-breeding purple pea plants (PP) are crossed with white plants (pp), and the F1 plants are then crossed with each other. Among the purple-flowered F2 plants, what fraction is expected to be heterozygous?
w: Step 1: the F1 are all Pp, and Pp x Pp gives 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp. Step 2: the purple plants are the PP and Pp groups (3 parts), and 2 of those 3 parts are Pp, so 2/3.

n.0: 3/4 is the fraction of all F2 plants that are purple.
n.2: 1/2 is the fraction of all F2 plants that are Pp; the question asks only about the purple ones.
n.3: 1/4 is the fraction of F2 plants that are PP (or that are white), not heterozygous purple.

q: For a gene with complete dominance, A is dominant over a. Which crosses can produce offspring showing the recessive phenotype? Select all that apply.
o: aa x aa
AA x AA
AA x aa
Aa x aa
AA x Aa
Aa x Aa
w: A recessive phenotype needs aa, so each parent must be able to pass on a. Aa x Aa (1/4 aa), Aa x aa (1/2 aa) and aa x aa (all aa) can all produce it.

n.1: AA x AA gives only AA offspring.
n.2: AA x aa gives only Aa offspring, all showing the dominant phenotype.
n.4: AA x Aa gives AA and Aa offspring; the AA parent always passes on A.

q: Two parents are both carriers of cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive disorder. What is the probability that their next child will also be a carrier? Enter your answer as a whole-number percent.

tr.25: gave the chance of an affected (ff) child
tr.67: gave the carrier share among unaffected children only
tr.75: gave the chance of an unaffected child

w: Ff x Ff gives 1 FF : 2 Ff : 1 ff. Carriers are Ff, so the probability is 2/4 = 1/2 = 50%.

q: In pea plants, round seeds (R) are dominant over wrinkled (r) and yellow (Y) over green (y), on different chromosomes. If RrYy x RrYy produces 160 offspring, how many are expected to be round and yellow? Enter a whole number.
w: Step 1: a dihybrid cross gives a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotype ratio, so 9/16 show both dominant traits. Step 2: 160 x 9/16 = 90.

q: Two parents are both heterozygous (Aa) for an autosomal recessive condition. What is the probability that their next two children will both be affected? Enter your answer as a percent, rounded to the nearest hundredth.

tr.25: gave the chance for one child
tr.50: added the two probabilities instead of multiplying

w: Step 1: each child has a 1/4 chance of being aa. Step 2: both events must happen (AND), so multiply: 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16 = 0.0625 = 6.25%.

q: A gardener crosses a red-flowered snapdragon with a white-flowered snapdragon, and every offspring plant has pink flowers. Which inheritance pattern does this show?
o: Codominance
Polygenic inheritance
Incomplete dominance
X-linked inheritance
w: In incomplete dominance the heterozygote shows a blended, intermediate phenotype: red x white gives pink.

n.0: In codominance both alleles show fully (red and white patches or hairs), not a blend.
n.1: Polygenic traits come from many genes and give a continuous range, not one uniform intermediate color.
n.3: X-linked inheritance concerns genes on the X chromosome; plants such as snapdragons do not have one.

q: A cross between a red-haired bull and a white-haired cow produces roan calves, whose coats contain a mixture of separate red hairs and white hairs. Which pattern of inheritance explains the roan coat?
o: Incomplete dominance
Multiple alleles
Sex-linked inheritance
Codominance
w: In codominance both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote; roan cattle show both red hairs and white hairs side by side.

n.0: Incomplete dominance would give a single blended color (for example, pink hairs), not separate red and white hairs.
n.1: Multiple alleles means more than two alleles in the population; only two (red and white) are involved here.
n.2: Coat color here is inherited the same way in both sexes; the cross does not involve a sex-chromosome pattern.

q: A father with type A blood (genotype IAi) and a mother with type B blood (genotype IBi) are expecting a child. Which blood types are possible for the child?
o: A and B, but not AB or O
A, B and AB, but not O
AB and O, but not A or B
A, B, AB and O
w: IAi x IBi gives IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B) and ii (O), each with a probability of 1/4.

n.0: This leaves out IAIB (AB) and ii (O), which are both possible because each parent can pass on either allele.
n.1: This leaves out type O; each parent carries i, so an ii child is possible.
n.2: This leaves out type A (IAi) and type B (IBi), which are also possible.

q: A genetics counselor reviews the ABO blood types of four couples. Which couple cannot have a child with type O blood?
o: Type AB (IAIB) and type O (ii)
Type A (IAi) and type O (ii)
Type A (IAi) and type B (IBi)
Type O (ii) and type O (ii)
w: A type O child must be ii, receiving i from each parent. A type AB parent (IAIB) has no i allele, so this couple can have only A (IAi) or B (IBi) children.

n.1: Both parents carry i, so an ii child (1/2 chance) is possible.
n.2: Both parents carry i, so an ii child (1/4 chance) is possible.
n.3: ii x ii gives ii children, all type O.

q: A student is reviewing how the three ABO alleles (IA, IB and i) interact. Which statement about the ABO blood group system is accurate?
o: IA is dominant over IB, so a person with IAIB is type A.
IA and IB blend by incomplete dominance into type AB.
The i allele is dominant, so type O is the most common.
The i allele is recessive to both the IA and IB alleles.
w: ABO shows multiple alleles: IA and IB are codominant with each other, and both are dominant over i. Type O requires ii.

n.0: IA and IB are codominant; a person with IAIB expresses both and is type AB.
n.1: Type AB shows both A and B antigens fully, which is codominance, not a blend.
n.2: i is recessive. A person must have two copies (ii) to be type O.

q: A man with red-green color blindness, an X-linked recessive trait, has children with a woman who carries no color-blindness allele. Which outcome is expected?
o: Half of the sons are color-blind and half of the daughters are carriers.
All of the daughters are carriers and none of the sons are color-blind.
Half of the daughters are color-blind and none of the sons are affected.
All of the sons are color-blind and none of the daughters are carriers.
w: Step 1: the father passes his X (with the allele) to every daughter and his Y to every son. Step 2: daughters get a normal X from the mother, so all are carriers; sons get the mother's normal X, so none are affected.

n.0: This is the pattern for a carrier mother and a normal father, not an affected father and a noncarrier mother.
n.2: Each daughter gets a normal X from her mother, which masks the recessive allele, so she is a carrier, not affected.
n.3: Sons receive the father's Y, not his X, so they cannot inherit his X-linked allele.

q: Hemophilia A is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. Why is the disorder seen much more often in males than in females?
o: Males have one X, so one recessive allele is expressed.
Males inherit the allele from their fathers.
The allele is carried on the Y chromosome.
The allele acts as dominant in males and recessive in females.
w: Males (XY) have only one X chromosome (hemizygous), so a single recessive allele on it is expressed. Females need two copies to be affected.

n.1: Sons get their X from their mother; the father gives sons his Y.
n.2: The gene is on the X chromosome. Y-linked traits pass only from father to son.
n.3: The allele is recessive in both sexes; males show it because they have no second X to mask it.

q: Adult height in a population forms a smooth bell-shaped range rather than a few distinct categories, and it is also affected by childhood nutrition. Which explanation best fits this pattern?
o: Codominance between two alleles of one gene
Incomplete dominance at a single gene locus
Polygenic inheritance, with environmental effects
Multiple alleles of one gene, with one dominant
w: Polygenic traits are controlled by many genes whose effects add up, producing a continuous range; environment such as nutrition also affects the phenotype.

n.0: Codominance at one gene gives a few distinct phenotypes, such as types A, B and AB, not a smooth range.
n.1: Incomplete dominance at one gene gives three phenotypes (such as red, pink and white), not a continuous range.
n.3: Multiple alleles at one gene still give a few separate categories, as in the four ABO blood types.

q: In a family pedigree, two unaffected parents have a daughter who is affected by a rare genetic disorder. Which inheritance pattern and parental genotypes best fit this pedigree?
o: Autosomal dominant, with one parent a carrier
Autosomal recessive, with both parents carriers
Y-linked, passed from the father to the daughter
X-linked recessive, with the mother a carrier
w: Step 1: unaffected parents with an affected child means the trait is recessive and both parents carry it. Step 2: an affected daughter with an X-linked recessive trait would need an affected father, and this father is unaffected, so the pattern is autosomal recessive.

n.0: In autosomal dominant inheritance anyone with one copy is affected, so an affected child needs an affected parent.
n.2: Y-linked traits pass from father to son; daughters do not receive a Y chromosome.
n.3: For a daughter to have an X-linked recessive trait she needs the allele from her father too, which would make him affected.

q: A genetics handout lists inherited disorders by pattern of inheritance. Which disorders are inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern? Select all that apply.
o: Cystic fibrosis
Huntington disease
Red-green color blindness
Sickle cell disease
Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Hemophilia A
w: Hemophilia A, red-green color blindness and Duchenne muscular dystrophy are X-linked recessive, which is why they are far more common in males.

n.0: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive; it affects males and females equally.
n.1: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant.
n.3: Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive.

q: A woman who is a carrier of hemophilia A (XHXh) and a man without hemophilia (XHY) plan a family. What percentage of their sons are expected to have hemophilia? Enter a whole-number percent.

tr.0: assumed a son inherits X-linked alleles from the father
tr.25: gave the share of all children affected, not of sons
tr.100: assumed every son of a carrier is affected

w: Sons get the Y from the father and one X from the mother. Half of the mother's eggs carry Xh, so 1/2 = 50% of sons (XhY) are expected to have hemophilia.

q: In snapdragons, flower color shows incomplete dominance: red (RR), pink (RW) and white (WW). Two pink plants are crossed and produce 240 seedlings. How many seedlings are expected to have pink flowers? Enter a whole number.

tr.60: gave the red or the white class
tr.180: used the 3:1 ratio of complete dominance

w: RW x RW gives 1 RR : 2 RW : 1 WW, so 2/4 = 1/2 are pink. 240 x 1/2 = 120.

q: After a large meal, a person's liver and skeletal muscles store excess glucose as a highly branched polysaccharide. Which molecule is formed?
o: Glycogen
Starch
Cellulose
Chitin
w: Animals store glucose as glycogen in the liver and muscles. Starch is the plant storage form.

n.1: Starch is the storage polysaccharide of plants, not animals.
n.2: Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide in plant cell walls.
n.3: Chitin is a structural polysaccharide in fungal walls and insect exoskeletons.

q: A lab analysis shows that an unknown macromolecule from a cell contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, but no phosphorus. Which type of macromolecule is it most likely to be?
o: A nucleic acid
A protein
A carbohydrate
A phospholipid
w: Step 1: nitrogen rules out carbohydrates and simple fats. Step 2: the absence of phosphorus rules out nucleic acids and phospholipids, leaving protein (C, H, O, N, often S).

n.0: Nucleic acids contain phosphorus in their phosphate groups.
n.2: Common carbohydrates such as sugars, starch and glycogen contain only C, H and O, so nitrogen points away from them.
n.3: Phospholipids contain a phosphate group, so phosphorus would be present.

q: Butter is solid at room temperature, while olive oil is liquid. Which difference in their fatty acids best explains this?
o: Butter's fats contain more glycerol molecules per fatty acid.
Olive oil's fatty acids carry more hydrogen atoms per carbon.
Butter's fatty acids are mostly saturated and pack tightly together.
Butter's fatty acids have more C=C double bonds, which form kinks.
w: Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds, so their straight chains pack tightly and the fat is solid. Unsaturated fatty acids in oils have double bonds that kink the chains.

n.0: Every triglyceride has one glycerol and three fatty acids; the difference is saturation.
n.1: This is reversed: saturated fatty acids such as butter's carry the most hydrogen. Olive oil's C=C double bonds mean fewer hydrogens.
n.3: This is reversed: double bonds and kinks belong to unsaturated fats, which are liquid.

q: Two glucose molecules are joined to form the disaccharide maltose. Which description of this reaction is correct?
o: A water molecule is released, forming a peptide bond.
A water molecule is released, forming a glycosidic bond.
A water molecule is added, forming a peptide bond.
A water molecule is added, forming a glycosidic bond.
w: Monomers are joined by dehydration synthesis, which releases water. Bonds between sugars are glycosidic bonds.

n.0: Peptide bonds join amino acids, not sugars.
n.2: This combines both errors: adding water breaks bonds, and peptide bonds join amino acids.
n.3: Adding water is hydrolysis, which breaks polymers apart rather than joining them.

q: A patient with lactose intolerance makes too little lactase. When lactase does digest lactose, which two monosaccharides are released?
o: Glucose and galactose
Galactose and fructose
Glucose and glucose
Glucose and fructose
w: Lactose (milk sugar) = glucose + galactose. Lactase hydrolyzes it into those two monosaccharides.

n.1: Galactose + fructose is not one of the common dietary disaccharides.
n.2: Glucose + glucose make maltose.
n.3: Glucose + fructose make sucrose (table sugar).

q: The rate of a human enzyme-catalyzed reaction rises as the temperature increases from 20 °C to 37 °C, then drops sharply at 50 °C. What best explains the drop?
o: The heat raises the activation energy of the reaction.
The enzyme denatures, and its active site loses its shape.
The enzyme is used up as it converts more of the substrate.
The heat breaks the peptide bonds in the enzyme's chain.
w: Above its optimum (about 37 °C for most human enzymes) the enzyme denatures: its folding is disrupted, the active site changes shape, and the substrate no longer fits.

n.0: Enzymes work by lowering activation energy. The drop is due to loss of enzyme shape, not a change in activation energy.
n.2: Enzymes are catalysts and are not consumed by the reactions they speed up.
n.3: Denaturation disrupts folding; the peptide bonds of the primary sequence stay intact.

q: In liver cells, the enzyme catalase greatly speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. How does catalase increase the reaction rate?
o: It increases the total energy the reaction releases.
It is consumed and becomes part of the products.
It shifts the equilibrium toward more products.
It lowers the activation energy of the reaction.
w: Enzymes are biological catalysts: they lower activation energy, are not consumed, and do not change the overall energy released.

n.0: Enzymes do not change the overall energy change of the reaction, only the energy needed to start it.
n.1: Enzymes are not consumed; they are released unchanged and reused.
n.2: Enzymes do not change the equilibrium of a reaction; they help it reach equilibrium faster.

q: Pepsin digests protein in the stomach, where the pH is about 2. If pepsin passes into the small intestine, where the pH is about 8, what will most likely happen to its activity?
o: It will fall, since pH 8 is far from pepsin's optimum.
It will stay the same, since pH does not affect enzymes.
It will rise, since trypsin activates pepsin at pH 8.
