It will rise, since enzymes work faster in basic solutions.
w: Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Pepsin works best near pH 2, so at pH 8 its shape changes and activity falls. Trypsin, with an optimum near pH 8, works in the small intestine.

n.1: pH strongly affects enzyme shape and activity.
n.2: Trypsin is a separate protein-digesting enzyme with its own optimum; it does not boost pepsin.
n.3: Enzymes do not all work faster in basic conditions; each has its own optimum, and pepsin's is acidic.

q: A drug molecule shaped like an enzyme's substrate binds to the active site and slows the reaction. Adding much more substrate restores the normal rate. Which type of inhibition is this?
o: Noncompetitive inhibition
Competitive inhibition
Substrate saturation
Denaturation by heat
w: A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and competes with the substrate, so raising substrate concentration can overcome it.

n.0: A noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the enzyme's shape; extra substrate does not overcome it.
n.2: Saturation is the plateau reached when all active sites are busy; it is not inhibition.
n.3: Denaturation is loss of enzyme shape from heat or extreme pH, not binding of an inhibitor.

q: When phospholipids are placed in water, they arrange themselves into a double layer. Which feature of phospholipid structure explains this arrangement?
o: Their tails are polar and are attracted to the surrounding water.
Their hydrophilic heads face water while hydrophobic tails face inward.
Their three fatty acid tails make them dissolve in water.
Their nonpolar heads face water while polar tails face inward.
w: A phospholipid has a hydrophilic (polar) phosphate head and two hydrophobic (nonpolar) fatty acid tails. In water the heads face outward and the tails hide inside, forming a bilayer.

n.0: The fatty acid tails are nonpolar and hydrophobic, so they avoid water.
n.2: Phospholipids have two fatty acid tails (triglycerides have three), and the tails repel water.
n.3: Polarity is reversed: the heads are polar and the tails are nonpolar.

q: A nutrition student is classifying carbohydrates found in foods and in the body. Which of these are polysaccharides? Select all that apply.
o: Glycogen
Starch
Lactose
Cellulose
Sucrose
Glucose
w: Starch (plant storage), glycogen (animal storage) and cellulose (plant cell walls) are polysaccharides, long chains of glucose units.

n.2: Lactose is a disaccharide (glucose + galactose).
n.5: Glucose is a monosaccharide, the monomer of these polysaccharides.

q: Place the levels of protein structure in order, starting with the simplest level and ending with the most complex.
o: R-group interactions fold the chain into its overall 3-D shape.
Hydrogen bonds along the backbone form helices and pleated sheets.
Amino acids are linked in a specific sequence by peptide bonds.
Two or more folded polypeptide chains join, as in hemoglobin.
w: Primary (amino acid sequence) -> secondary (alpha helix and beta pleated sheet from backbone hydrogen bonds) -> tertiary (overall 3-D shape from R-group interactions) -> quaternary (two or more chains, such as the four chains of hemoglobin).

q: A college student with a common cold caused by a rhinovirus asks a clinic nurse for an antibiotic. Which statement best explains why an antibiotic will not help?
o: Viruses are not cells and lack the targets antibiotics act on.
Viruses are prokaryotic cells whose walls block antibiotics.
Rhinoviruses multiply too fast for antibiotics to act.
Rhinoviruses are bacteria that have become drug resistant.
w: Antibiotics kill or inhibit bacteria by acting on bacterial structures and processes. Viruses are not cells (no cell wall, ribosomes or metabolism of their own), so antibiotics have no effect on them.

n.1: Viruses are not cells at all, prokaryotic or otherwise, and they have no cell wall.
n.2: Speed of replication is not the problem. Antibiotics have no bacterial target to act on in a virus, however slowly it multiplies.
n.3: Rhinoviruses are viruses, not bacteria, so antibiotic resistance does not apply to them.

q: Researchers isolate a new bacterium from every sick animal in an outbreak and grow it in pure culture. According to Koch's postulates, what should they do next?
o: Treat the sick animals with an antibiotic and record recovery.
Re-isolate the bacterium from a newly infected animal.
Find the bacterium in each diseased animal in the outbreak.
Introduce the cultured bacterium into a healthy animal.
w: Koch's postulates: (1) the microbe is found in all diseased hosts, (2) it is isolated and grown in pure culture, (3) it causes the disease when introduced into a healthy host, (4) it is re-isolated from that host. Steps 1 and 2 are done, so step 3 is next.

n.0: Treating with antibiotics is not one of Koch's postulates and would not show that the microbe causes the disease.
n.1: Re-isolating the microbe is the final step (4); it can only follow infection of a healthy host.
n.2: Finding the microbe in all diseased hosts is step 1, which the researchers have already done.

q: A traveler returns from a tropical region with cycles of fever and chills and is diagnosed with malaria. Which statement correctly identifies the cause and how it spread?
o: A bacterium, spread through contaminated drinking water
A bacterium, spread by the bite of infected deer ticks
A virus, spread by the bite of Anopheles mosquitoes
A protozoan, spread by the bite of Anopheles mosquitoes
w: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium, a single-celled eukaryote. The female Anopheles mosquito is the vector that carries it, not the cause.

n.0: Malaria is vector-borne; waterborne protozoan illness is giardiasis.
n.1: Ticks spread Lyme disease, caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, not malaria.
n.2: The mosquito is the correct vector, but the pathogen is a protozoan, not a virus.

q: A high school wrestler develops a red, ring-shaped, scaly rash and is diagnosed with tinea corporis (ringworm). Which type of medication is appropriate for this infection?
o: An antiviral
An antibiotic for bacteria
An antihelminthic for worms
An antifungal
w: Despite its name, ringworm (tinea) is a fungal skin infection, so it is treated with an antifungal.

n.0: Antivirals target viruses; tinea is caused by a fungus.
n.1: Antibiotics target bacteria; tinea is caused by a fungus.
n.2: Ringworm is not caused by a worm; the name comes from the ring-shaped rash.

q: A sample of bacteria from a patient's wound is Gram stained and appears purple under the microscope. What does this result indicate about the bacteria?
o: Gram-negative, with an outer lipid membrane
Gram-negative, with a thick peptidoglycan wall
Gram-positive, with a thin wall and outer membrane
Gram-positive, with a thick peptidoglycan wall
w: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall that holds the purple (violet) stain. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin wall plus an outer membrane and stain pink or red.

n.0: An outer membrane is the Gram-negative feature, and those bacteria stain pink, not purple.
n.1: Gram-negative bacteria stain pink and have a thin peptidoglycan layer, not a thick one.
n.2: A thin wall with an outer membrane is the Gram-negative structure, which does not stain purple.

q: A hospital places a patient with active tuberculosis in a negative-pressure room and staff wear fitted respirators. Which feature of tuberculosis transmission explains these precautions?
o: TB spreads mainly on objects such as bed rails and doorknobs.
TB bacteria travel in tiny particles that stay suspended in air.
TB is caused by a virus that passes through surgical masks.
TB spreads mainly in large droplets that fall within 2 meters.
w: Tuberculosis (bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis) is spread by the airborne route: tiny particles stay suspended and travel on air currents, so airflow control and respirators are needed.

n.0: Spread by contaminated objects (fomites) would call for surface cleaning, not special airflow; TB spreads through the air.
n.2: Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium, not a virus.
n.3: Large droplets that fall within about 1 to 2 meters describe droplet spread, as with influenza; TB is airborne.

q: Before giving an injection, a nurse cleans the patient's skin with an alcohol-based solution to reduce the number of microbes. What is this practice called?
o: Sterilization
Antisepsis
Disinfection
Pasteurization
w: Antisepsis reduces microbes on living tissue such as skin. Disinfection is for objects and surfaces.

n.0: Sterilization kills all microbes including endospores (as in an autoclave) and is not done on skin.
n.2: Disinfection reduces pathogens on objects and surfaces, not on living tissue.
n.3: Pasteurization is gentle heating of foods such as milk, not skin preparation.

q: After a long course of a broad-spectrum antibiotic, a patient develops severe diarrhea caused by an overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile in the colon. Which explanation is most likely?
o: The antibiotic converted harmless gut bacteria into C. difficile.
The antibiotic killed normal gut bacteria that kept C. difficile in check.
The antibiotic caused the patient's own colon cells to divide rapidly.
The antibiotic weakened the colon wall, letting viruses enter.
w: Normal microbiota compete with pathogens. Killing them with an antibiotic lets an opportunistic pathogen such as C. difficile overgrow.

n.0: Antibiotics kill or inhibit bacteria; they do not turn one bacterial species into another.
n.2: The diarrhea is caused by an overgrowing pathogen, not by the patient's own cells dividing.
n.3: C. difficile is a bacterium, and the disease here is bacterial overgrowth, not viral entry.

q: A patient stops taking a prescribed antibiotic after three days because she feels better. Why can this practice contribute to antibiotic resistance?
o: The drug makes each bacterium change to resist it.
Her body itself becomes resistant to the antibiotic.
Viruses in her body learn to resist antibiotics.
Surviving bacteria tend to be the most resistant ones.
w: An incomplete course kills the most susceptible bacteria first; the survivors are more likely to carry resistance, and they multiply. This is natural selection, and resistance genes can also spread on plasmids.

n.0: Antibiotics do not make bacteria change on purpose; they select bacteria that already carry resistance.
n.1: Resistance is a property of the bacteria, not of the patient's body.
n.2: Antibiotics do not act on viruses, so viral resistance to them is not the issue.

q: An infection-control handout groups diseases by the type of pathogen that causes them. Which of these diseases are caused by bacteria? Select all that apply.
o: Lyme disease
Malaria
Tuberculosis
Strep throat
Influenza
Athlete's foot
w: Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi, spread by ticks) and strep throat (Streptococcus pyogenes) are bacterial.

n.1: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium.
n.4: Influenza is caused by a virus.
n.5: Athlete's foot is caused by a fungus.

q: Place the links in the chain of infection in order, starting with the infectious agent and ending with the person who becomes infected.
o: Mode of transmission
Susceptible host
Infectious agent
Reservoir
Portal of exit
Portal of entry
w: The pathogen (infectious agent) lives in a reservoir, leaves through a portal of exit, travels by a mode of transmission, enters a new host through a portal of entry, and infects a susceptible host. Breaking any link stops the spread.

q: Place the stages of viral replication in the order they occur when an influenza virus infects a host cell, starting with the first.
o: New virus particles are assembled.
The virus attaches to receptors on the host cell.
New virus particles are released from the cell.
The viral genome is copied and viral proteins are made.
The virus or its genome enters the host cell.
w: Viruses replicate only inside host cells: attachment -> entry -> copying of the viral genome and synthesis of viral proteins on the host's ribosomes -> assembly -> release.
